newsitem.title: USA: Wall St lifts 1997 corporate profit sights.
newsitem.headline: Wall St lifts 1997 corporate profit sights.

text.p: A surprisingly strong fourth quarter performance by the largest companies in the U.S. has led several Wall Street firms to acknowledge their outlook for the coming year was too gloomy.

Last week, Salomon Brothers' U.S. equity strategist David Shulman increased his 1997 estimate for operating earnings of the Standard & Poor's 500 companies, citing preliminary fourth quarter 1996 data. Today, Merrill Lynch and Dean Witter weighed in, with Merrill also boosting its number and Dean Witter placing its estimate under review.

"Fourth quarter earnings were a blow out," Merrill said in a statement. The firm now expects S&P 500 companies will earn an aggregate of $44 per share in 1997, a six percent rise over its 1996 estimate of $41.40 per share.

The number puts Merrill in line with Salomon strategist Shluman, who likewise now sees S&P 500 earnings of $44 per share for the year, a 7.3 percent rise compared with his $41 per share estimate for 1996.
Dean Witter left unchanged its 1997 outlook, pending a review, but that firm was already anticipating a $44 per share year for the S&P 500 even without the fourth quarter data.
To be sure, there were weak spots in the quarter.
"Notably, the record pace of favorable earnings surprises stalled last week," Dean Witter investment strategist Scott Reed said in a research note.

"However, in aggregate, fourth quarter 1996 earnings are still coming in well above Street expectations, and this brief deterioration in profit reports has not altered our favorable earnings outlook for 1997," he said.

The improved earnings outlook is good news for equity investors. Many firms, Merrill included, have advised investors to shift some assets to bonds and away from stocks, often citing the slow-growth outlook for corporate earnings.
Interpreted at the most basic level, the higher estimates mean stock prices represent a lower multiple to earnings than previously thought.

Even after taking into account the strong fourth quarter, however, Merrill remained cautious in its comments, warning its new estimate still represents a sharp slowdown from five straight years of double-digit growth.
Also, Merrill's 1998 estimate stands at $45.50 per share, which would amount to only three percent growth.

Salomon Brothers is using a $46 estimate for 1998, for about 4.5 percent growth, and Dean Witter remains the most bullish of the pack with a preliminary estimate of $46.65, or six percent over 1997 levels.
